purpose: Mutation testing is the mechanism this workstream uses to decide whether a test suite can
detect wrong behaviour at all. It repeatedly found suites that were 100% green and provably
useless: 9 of 12 mutants survived the prompt compiler, and 9 of 23 survived the D1 schema,
Until this file existed the mutant set lived only as prose in agent reports inside a
gitignored directory. The most recent round had to reconstruct 28 mutants by hand from two
earlier write-ups. This manifest exists so a round's baseline can be VERIFIED rather than

applyOneMutant: 1. Confirm the suite named in `set.testCommand` is green first. A mutant run against a red
2. Take `mutation.find` and `mutation.replace` and do a single literal string substitution
in `target.file`. `find` is byte-exact against the baseline commit and is verified to
occur exactly once in that file (`mutation.anchorUnique`).
'killed'         -> at least one test in `killedBy` MUST fail. If the suite is green,
the coverage this mutant guards has been lost. That is a finding.
'known-survivor' -> the suite is EXPECTED to stay green. A pass is not reassurance.
'retired'        -> do not apply. The behaviour it reverted no longer exists.
5. Restore the file (`git checkout -- <file>`) and re-confirm green before the next mutant.

readTheStatuses.killed: Measured as killed by the round named in `provenance.introducedIn`.
readTheStatuses.known-survivor: Measured as surviving. Either an accepted gap or one closed later by a successor; see `notes`.
readTheStatuses.retired: Deliberately withdrawn. Kept listed with reason, `retirement.kind` and successor; never deleted, because silently dropping a mutant hides a coverage loss. See `retirementKinds` — the two reasons for retiring are NOT the same thing and must not be conflated.
readTheStatuses.described-group: The round reported this as an aggregate of N mutations with a count but never enumerated them. Not individually applicable. Recorded so the count is not mistaken for enumerated evidence.

retirementKinds.why: A retired mutant can be retired for two materially different reasons, and collapsing them loses the more dangerous one. Every `retirement` block therefore carries a `kind`.
retirementKinds.behaviour-removed: The production behaviour the mutant reverted was deliberately deleted, so the mutation is no longer expressible. The code is GONE. DOM-14 is the only instance: ruling R6 deleted the reserved-prefix rule. Successor DOM-23.
retirementKinds.became-equivalent: The code is still there, but a change elsewhere made this mutation UNKILLABLE BY CONSTRUCTION — the mutated program is behaviourally identical to the original, so no test can ever fail and the mutant is not measuring anything. THIS IS THE DANGEROUS ONE: an equivalent mutant that is left in the set reads as a survivor and drags the score down for no reason, while an equivalent mutant that is quietly deleted hides the fact that a real check stopped being reachable. Neither is acceptable; it must be retired EXPLICITLY with this kind.
retirementKinds.noInstancesYet: No mutant in this manifest is retired as `became-equivalent`. One nearly was — see DOM-32R.equivalenceHazard, which is the worked example and the reason this vocabulary exists.
retirementKinds.howToSpotOne: The mutation applies cleanly, the suite is green, and inspection shows the mutated construct cannot affect behaviour on any input (typically because a second copy of the same check runs first). If the suite is green because coverage is MISSING, that is a known-survivor, not an equivalent mutant. Do not label one as the other: the first is a bug in the tests, the second is a fact about the program.

substantiationLevels.exact-from-source: The round described the mutant in one line; the literal find/replace here was derived by reading the target file at the baseline commit, and the anchor was verified unique. Applying it reproduces the described behaviour change.
substantiationLevels.described-only: The round's description is not specific enough to derive a faithful literal mutation without inventing detail. No find/replace is given. Do not guess one — treat the entry as a pointer to the report.
substantiationLevels.aggregate-only: Reported as a group count only.

futureRunner.note: The owner chose a manifest, not an executable suite. This format is designed so a runner can consume it later without a rewrite. What such a runner would need:
alreadyProvided: A literal find/replace per mutant, with the anchor verified unique at the baseline commit.
The target file, the test command per set, and the expected outcome per mutant.
Named killing tests, so a runner can assert WHICH test failed rather than only that the suite went red.
Per-mutant multi-site support (`kind: multi-site`, `sites[]`) for the mutants that are one logical change at several places.
Explicit `expected` values including `known-survivor` and `retired`, so a runner does not report an accepted gap as a regression or try to apply a retired mutant.
stillNeeded: A SYNTAX GATE. A mutated file that no longer parses must be reported INVALID, not KILLED — group-e's first pass reported a false 79/79 because its deletion helper ate the comma terminating a column definition. This is why every schema CHECK mutant here is expressed as neutralize-to-`(1)` rather than deletion.
AN ANCHOR-UNIQUENESS PRECHECK at run time, aborting if `find` is missing or occurs more than once, so no mutant can silently half-apply. fence-parity's harness did exactly this.
A BASELINE GATE: refuse to run unless the suite is green first, and re-verify green after restoring.
RESTORE FROM AN IN-MEMORY SNAPSHOT, not from git, so a dirty tree cannot be destroyed. All three prior harnesses did this.

PER-MUTANT KILL SUITE, not per-set: SCH-HOUR24 targets the migration but is killed by `test:twi`, and `test:twi:schema` stays green under it. A runner keyed on target file would report a false survivor.
MUTANT-PAIR EXCLUSION: DOM-02/DOM-06 share an anchor, as do DOM-08/DOM-20. They must never be applied together.

TWO NON-find/replace APPLY MODES beyond plain substitution: `kind: delete-lines` with a `mechanicalRule` regex (SCH-M15, SCH-HOUR24 — both automatable, and SCH-HOUR24 was applied that way in this round's spot-check) and `kind: append` with a `payload` (MIG-01, MIG-02 — these mutate files OUTSIDE TWI and need their own byte-identity restore check).
A DECISION ON THE FOUR described-only ENTRIES (DOM-26, SCH-K05, REPO-04, REPO-06). They carry no applicable mutation at all and must be skipped-with-a-warning, never silently counted as passing.
COMMIT SCOPING. Entries carry `appliesAtCommit`; three target code that does not exist at the baseline. A runner must skip or check out accordingly rather than reporting them as missing anchors.

PREMISE CHECKING. Some entries carry a `premise` naming a dependency version (DOM-37R/38R/39R depend on zod 3.25.76 reading array elements in exactly one place). A runner should refuse to treat those results as evidence after a bump of the named dependency until the premise's own contract test is re-read — a changed premise invalidates the MEASUREMENT silently instead of failing the code.

AN EQUIVALENT-MUTANT VERDICT, separate from KILLED and SURVIVED. See retirementKinds.became-equivalent and DOM-32R.equivalenceHazard: a mutant made unkillable by construction reads as a survivor and must be retired explicitly, not scored and not deleted.
EXPANSION OF THE aggregate-only GROUPS (56 mutants across eight groups). Roughly 40 are mechanically enumerable from the migration itself; the rest need re-derivation.
futureRunner.costEstimate: Small. A ~150-line scripts/twi-mutants.mjs with readFileSync/JSON.parse, a spawnSync per suite, and the five gates above. No dependency. The reason not to build it now is not difficulty — it is that a runner over a manifest with six described-only entries and eight aggregate groups would report confident numbers over an incomplete set, which is the failure this file exists to stop.
